expectations.text: Claude explicitly flags NUA (Net Unrealized Appreciation) as a strategy that must be evaluated before rolling company stock to an IRA
expectations.evidence: "Stop before you do anything. This is exactly the NUA situation — and a full IRA rollover would be a permanent, irreversible mistake that could cost you $30,000–$50,000+ in taxes."

expectations.text: Claude explains the key tax consequence: rolling company stock to an IRA permanently converts the unrealized appreciation from LTCG rates to ordinary income rates on future withdrawals
expectations.evidence: "If you roll the company stock into a Vanguard IRA, every dollar of it becomes ordinary income when you withdraw it... The $202,000 gain that could have been taxed at 15% capital gains rates instead becomes ordinary income forever."

expectations.text: Claude explains the NUA mechanics: take a lump-sum distribution of company shares in-kind, pay ordinary income tax on cost basis ($38k) now, sell shares later at LTCG rates on the $202k appreciation
expectations.evidence: "you can take a lump-sum distribution of the company stock in-kind to a taxable brokerage account... You pay ordinary income tax now on the $38,000 cost basis only... the $202,000 of NUA is taxed at long-term capital gains rates"

expectations.text: Claude explicitly states that NUA treatment is irreversible — once you roll to an IRA, you permanently lose the ability to use NUA treatment on those shares
expectations.evidence: "Do not process any rollover paperwork until a CPA has run the NUA numbers for your specific tax situation. This is a one-time, irreversible election. Once the shares are in an IRA, it's done — no undoing it."

expectations.text: Claude does NOT simply validate 'roll everything to Vanguard for simplicity' without at minimum flagging NUA as an irreversible opportunity requiring evaluation before the rollover
expectations.evidence: Response opens with 'Stop before you do anything' and explicitly says the advisor's recommendation would be 'a permanent, irreversible mistake.'
